title: Iterators & Generators
blurb: Master the two-method protocol, generators that pause, and lazy pipelines whose work happens only when someone asks.

cells.title: The protocol: __iter__ plus __next__
cells.body:
Every for loop in Python is a client of a two-method protocol. __iter__ says 'hand out the iterator' — for an iterator object it just returns self. __next__ produces the next value, and signals exhaustion by raising StopIteration; once raised, it should keep raising. The for statement calls iter() once, then next() repeatedly, catching StopIteration internally so your code never sees it.

Writing one iterator class by hand teaches you what generators do for free — and it lets you add protocol-visible features generators cannot easily offer, like reset(), because the state is explicit fields on self. The discipline: decide exactly what 'the next value' means and when 'done' happens, and make __next__ answer both questions identically on every call, even after exhaustion.

cells.title: Generators: functions that pause mid-sentence
cells.body:
A function containing yield is a generator function: calling it runs none of the body. You get back a generator object, and each next() runs the body forward to the next yield, hands out the value, and freezes — local variables, loop counters and the instruction pointer all survive the pause. When the body falls off the end, the generator raises StopIteration automatically.

The pause is not a curiosity; it is the execution model to reason about. Side effects (a print, an append to a log) inside a generator happen at consumption time, not at definition time, and a generator is one-shot: exhausted is exhausted. Predicting when each line runs is the actual skill this notebook drills — it is the same skill you need to debug lazy pipelines and streaming code later.

demo.code:
def announce(n):
    print("  computing", n)
    return n


def stream():
    for i in range(3):
        print("about to yield", i)
        yield announce(i)


g = stream()
print("created; nothing ran yet")
print(next(g))
print(list(g))

cells.title: Infinite streams, bounded consumers
cells.body:
A while True loop inside a generator is perfectly safe — nothing runs until something pulls, and the puller decides when to stop. That inverts the usual shape of 'generate a big list, then slice it': instead you write an endless source and pair it with a bounded consumer. itertools.islice(gen, n) takes exactly n items; a for with a break takes items until a condition; sum() takes everything and reduces as it goes.

The design rule: the source knows how to produce the next item forever; policy — how many, until when, under what condition — belongs to the consumer. Splitting those concerns is what keeps memory constant and makes 'first n items satisfying P' a three-line program instead of a guessing game about upper bounds.

exercise.title: Draining the Tank
exercise.statement:
A mixing tank starts holding start units of water. Every cycle, the outlet reports the current level and then 3 units drain. The pump shuts off once the level would drop below zero — so the last reported level is the final non-negative one.

Write a generator tank_drain(start) that yields the levels one at a time (10, 7, 4, 1 for a tank of 10), plus the driver drain_log(start) — the function the tests call — which returns the complete list of yielded levels by consuming your generator.
constraints: levels are yielded in decreasing order, all >= 0
a tank at 0 still reports one level (0) before shutting off

examples.why: 10 drains to 7 to 4 to 1; the next step would be -2, so the pump stops
an empty tank still reports its single level

hints: Which loop shape reports the level BEFORE draining — and what condition makes it stop exactly when the next report would be negative?
Keep the level in one variable; while it is >= 0: yield it, then subtract 3. The generator body is four lines.
def tank_drain(start): level = start; while level >= 0: yield level; level -= 3 — then drain_log simply returns list(tank_drain(start)).
exercise.reasoning: The order of operations inside the loop body is the entire specification: yield first, drain second. Report-then-act is what makes a start level of 0 yield one value (0 is reported, then the pump would go negative) and a start of 2 yield exactly [2]. Writing the driver as list(...) of the generator is the idiomatic way to observe a stream — nothing is materialized until the list constructor pulls, which is exactly the consumption model generators promise. The same 'emit current state, then advance' pattern appears in every sequence-generating problem: get the order right and the boundary cases decide themselves.

exercise.title: Checkpoint Labels Forever
exercise.statement:
A race course has checkpoints labeled A1, B1, C1, A2, B2, C2, A3, ... — the letter cycles A, B, C and the number steps up after each C. The course is open indefinitely, and the timing system needs the first n labels on demand.

Write an infinite generator label_stream() (no arguments, never ends, never builds a list) that yields labels in order. Then write the tested driver checkpoint_labels(count): the first count labels, obtained by consuming the stream with a bounded consumer such as itertools.islice or repeated next() calls.
constraints: label_stream must yield labels one at a time, forever — no list, no upper bound
count = 0 must produce [] without pulling a label it does not need

examples.why: the letters cycle while the number is still 1 for the fourth label

exercise.starter:
from itertools import islice


def label_stream():
    """Yield A1, B1, C1, A2, B2, C2, ... forever, one at a time."""
    pass


def checkpoint_labels(count):
    """Return the first count labels from label_stream()."""
    pass
hints: The label needs two counters moving at different rates — when does the letter restart, and when does the number grow?
Nest two loops: an outer while True that holds the current number, and an inner for over 'ABC' that yields letter + str(number). After the inner loop finishes, the number increments.
In the driver, return list(islice(label_stream(), count)) — islice pulls exactly count values (and zero values when count is 0), so the infinite source is always safe.
exercise.reasoning: Two counters tick at different rates — the letter cycles every step, the number every three — and the generator shape makes the coupling obvious: the outer loop owns the slow counter (the number), the inner loop owns the fast one (the letters). Because the source is infinite and the consumer decides the bound, checkpoint_labels(0) and checkpoint_labels(500) are the same program with a different limit — no pre-sized buffer, no guessed maximum. This division of labor (endless source, bounded consumer) is the design you will reach for whenever 'how many' is a runtime question rather than a property of the data.

exercise.title: Proof of Laziness
exercise.statement:
Lazy pipelines have two properties people claim but rarely test: nothing happens until consumption, and for each element the filter clause runs before the output expression. You will build a pipeline that proves both, with an event log as the witness.

Implement pipeline_trace(numbers) — the tested function — exactly as follows. Create events = [] and a helper watch(value, tag) that appends tag + ":" + str(value) to events and returns the value. Build gen as a generator expression over numbers whose filter clause calls watch(x, "test") and keeps even values, and whose output expression calls watch(x * x, "map") and yields the square. Then record before = len(events), consume with consumed = list(gen), and return [before, consumed, events].
constraints: the pipeline must be a generator expression — building any intermediate list defeats the point
the filter must call watch for EVERY element; the map only for the survivors

examples.why: no events before consumption; per element the test fires first and the map only for evens
both elements pass, so every test is followed by its map

exercise.starter:
def pipeline_trace(numbers):
    """Prove laziness and clause order with an event log.

    events = [] and watch(value, tag) appends tag + ':' + str(value)
    and returns value. gen is a generator expression over numbers:
    filter clause watch(x, 'test') keeping evens, output expression
    watch(x * x, 'map'). Return [len(events) BEFORE consuming,
    list(gen), events AFTER].
    """
    pass
hints: If generator expressions were eager, what would len(events) be before list(gen)? What does the actual 0 prove?
The comprehension syntax order IS the evaluation order: for each element, the if clause evaluates first; the output expression runs only for survivors. Put watch exactly where each clause needs it.
gen = (watch(x * x, "map") for x in numbers if watch(x, "test") % 2 == 0) — then before = len(events); consumed = list(gen); return [before, consumed, events].
exercise.reasoning: The event log turns two invisible properties into data. before == 0 proves laziness: defining the generator expression ran none of its clauses, because a generator is a suspended computation until the first pull. The interleaving proves clause order: for each element the sequence is test then (only if kept) map — which is precisely how a hand-written loop with an if would behave, because comprehensions are loops in disguise. Once you can predict this trace, you can predict when side effects fire in any lazy pipeline — the exact skill that debugging dataflow code demands, where work happens at the consumer's pace, not the producer's.
exercise.solution:
def pipeline_trace(numbers):
    events = []

    def watch(value, tag):
        events.append(tag + ":" + str(value))
        return value

    gen = (watch(x * x, "map") for x in numbers if watch(x, "test") % 2 == 0)
    before = len(events)     # 0 — nothing has run yet
    consumed = list(gen)     # consumption drives every event
    return [before, consumed, events]

exercise.title: The Resettable Fib Counter
exercise.statement:
A step laboratory uses a mechanical counter that produces a Fibonacci-style sequence from two seeds: starting at (a, b) it yields a, b, a+b, b+(a+b), ... — every value is the sum of the previous two. The device has a lifetime budget: it yields at most limit values, and after that it is spent (further nexts raise StopIteration forever).

Implement FibCounter(a, b, limit) as a full iterator class: __iter__ returns self; __next__ returns the next value or raises StopIteration; reset(x, y) restarts from new seeds and restores the full limit. Then write the tested driver fib_session(a, b, limit, ops): ops are ["take", k] (record the next up-to-k values), ["skip", k] (advance up to k values, recording nothing) and ["reset", x, y]. It returns the flat list of recorded values.
constraints: take/skip past the limit simply run dry — no exception reaches the caller
a for-loop or islice over a FibCounter must work (that is what __iter__ is for)

examples.why: skip silently consumes 2 and 3, so the next take records 5 and 8

hints: Which three facts must __next__ consult before producing a value — how many have been given, what is the current pair, and what happens when the budget is spent?

Track _current, _following and _given. __next__ raises StopIteration when _given >= limit; otherwise returns _current, advances the pair, and increments _given. reset() restores the seeds AND zeroes _given.
In the driver use islice(counter, k) for both take (extend the recording) and skip (loop and discard). islice honors StopIteration, so running dry is just a short take — no exception handling needed.
exercise.reasoning: A hand-written iterator makes you own the three pieces of state that a generator would hide: the current pair (what the next two values are), the given count (how much of the budget is spent), and the exhaustion rule (_given >= limit raises, and keeps raising — a spent iterator must stay spent). The reset method is the feature a generator cannot cleanly offer: because the state is explicit fields, restarting is just writing them back, including restoring the full budget. The driver leans on the protocol itself: islice(counter, k) pulls through __next__ and stops at StopIteration, which is why 'take past the limit' needs no special case — the exhaustion rule and the bounded consumer agree on what happens at the end.
